newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU investors guarantee plan hijacked by German row.
newsitem.headline: EU investors guarantee plan hijacked by German row.

text.p: BRUSSELS, Nov 7 Reuter) - A plan to provide minimum protection for small European Union investors when an investment firm fails is bogged down in a legal dispute over similar rules covering bank deposits.

Final legislation on investor protection, which foresees minimum compensation of 20,000 European currency units ($25,380), should have been agreed months ago at a special meeting of EU finance ministers and European Parliament representatives.

But the parliament has so far refused to hold the meeting, preferring to wait until the European Court of Justice decides on a German bid to have the 1994 bank deposits directive outlawed, EU sources said.

In an unusual move, the German government took the Council of EU ministers and the parliament to court for adopting the directive against its will. The directive also provides minimum coverage of 20,000 Ecus for bank deposits when a failed firm's assets are not enough to cover for its liabilities.
Both protection plans are deemed necessary as banks and investment firms are free to offer their services throughout the 15-nation block.

The German problem is not that it opposes protecting small stock investors or bank depositors. In fact German banks and investment firms already provide a high level of protection in case of failure by one of their members.

But in a move to ensure that all banks on a given national territory -- be they domestic institutions or branches of foreign banks -- are on an equal footing, a majority of EU finance ministers agreed that higher national deposit guarantee schemes would not be exported abroad. This is the so-called non-export clause.
In the same spirit, they also agreed that foreign branches would be allowed to join host country schemes if they were more generous than their own -- the topping-up clause.
Germany strongly opposed both clauses arguing, in the second case, against offering protection to banks it does not control.

Under the rules of the EU's single market created in 1993, once a bank is authorised by its home country's supervising authority it can operate freely throughout the bloc. The same applies since January this year to investment firms.
The Court of Justice is not expected to rule on Germany's action before next spring at the earliest.
But on December 10 it should have the opinion of its advocate-general Philippe Leger, a Court official told Reuters. The Court usually follows the advocate-general's opinion.
It is most unlikely that any progress will be made on the protection of small stock investors until, at least, Leger has given his opinion on the deposit guarantee directive, EU sources said.
"It makes no sense convening a meeting...on the investors protection scheme until the court has ruled on the deposit guarantee directive," one source said. $1 = 0.78 Ecus
